title: I see you Rudra.
reviewNotes: Saved montage and captions reviewed, with full native later diagrams checked. Begin after ...f1=Q at 70 seconds in the complete nine-piece later diagram. Nb2 is certified against all twenty legal Black replies, each followed by an actual a4 or c4 mate. Selected source Qf2/a4 and independently supplied Qd1/c4 and c5/a4 illustrate the complete certificate. Earlier Nc6 sacrifice, declined-sacrifice branches and the route to promotion remain source context outside this proof. No larger-position engine estimate or tablebase claim is used.
transcript: Rudra will resign. Yes, you Rudra. I know what kind of man you are. You see that there is a black pawn that you cannot stop with your knight. Black is going to get a queen and win the game. And so you're just going to resign, right? But that would be a massive mistake because white does have a way >> [music] >> to win this position. And it all starts with the incredible and majestic knight to c6. A move that looks like the only blunder available in the position. The most interesting line happens after the knight is taken. So let me show you what happens if black doesn't take it. Of course the pawn cannot be pushed because there's going to be a knight fork and black [music] is going to lose the pawn on the next move. But I'm sure you had calculated that, right? And if the black king tries to run this way, now white can start eating up the pawns and move the knight to stop the pawn like this. And it doesn't matter that the king can attack the knight because the knight can stop the pawn like this and sacrifice itself. White is going to promote first and this is completely winning. But okay, what's the idea after black takes the knight? Surely now black is simply out of the woods. Well now white starts attacking the pawn with the knight. What? This doesn't make sense. We already saw that the pawn can simply run and the knight can never catch it. What is the point of this? Black can simply get a queen. And yes, that is true. But there is the incredibly precise and surprising knight to b2. And believe it or not, these black pawns are shielding the white king from queen checks. This queen has no way to prevent the push of [music] one of these two pawns, which is inevitably going to lead to a checkmate on the next move. So this is how you could have won this, Rudra. No matter where the queen goes on the next move, it is going to be a beautiful checkmate. Follow for more.
